s.u1.title: More food from the same land
s.u1.blurb: India has almost no new land left to farm, and a quarter of a billion tonnes of grain to find every year.
s.u2.title: Better seed
s.u2.blurb: Choosing what to plant, and how a variety with the characters you want gets made in the first place.
s.u3.title: Feeding the soil and watering it
s.u3.blurb: Sixteen nutrients, two ways of supplying them, and the water without which none of it matters.
s.u4.title: Arranging the crops, and keeping them
s.u4.blurb: What to plant beside what, and in what order. Then weeds, pests and the warehouse.
s.u5.title: Cattle and poultry
s.u5.blurb: Milk and draught, layers and broilers, and what good management actually consists of.

ch12.u1.problem:
India has more than a billion people and the number is still rising. Feeding them will take a quarter of a billion tonnes of grain every year.

There are two ways to get more grain: farm more land, or get more out of the land already being farmed. The first is nearly closed. India is already intensively cultivated and there is no large stock of new fields waiting.

So the whole chapter is about the second one: efficiency, on both crops and livestock.

It has been done before. The green revolution raised food-grain production and the white revolution did the same for milk. Between 1952 and 2010 grain production went up four times on only a quarter more cultivated land.

That came at a cost. Both revolutions used natural resources harder, and pushed further the same way damages soil, water and the balance that keeps them working. So the target is not simply more: it is more without wrecking what produces it. That is what sustainable means here.

One more thing is worth saying plainly. Filling warehouses does not end hunger on its own. People have to be able to buy the food, and most of the people who cannot are the ones who work in agriculture. Raising their income is part of the problem, which is why mixed farming, intercropping and integrated practices appear in a science chapter.
a.ch12-u1-read-1.title: The land is not getting any bigger
ch12.u1.sort.i0.label: Wheat, rice, maize, millets and sorghum
ch12.u1.sort.i0.why: The cereals. They carry most of the energy in an Indian diet.
ch12.u1.sort.i1.label: Gram, pea, black gram, green gram, pigeon pea and lentil
ch12.u1.sort.i1.why: The pulses: chana, matar, urad, moong, arhar and masoor.
ch12.u1.sort.i2.label: Soyabean, ground nut, sesame, castor, mustard, linseed and sunflower
ch12.u1.sort.i2.why: The oil seeds, which is where the cooking oil comes from.
ch12.u1.sort.i3.label: Vegetables, spices and fruits
ch12.u1.sort.i3.why: Plus small amounts of protein, carbohydrate and fat.
ch12.u1.sort.i4.label: Berseem, oats and sudan grass
ch12.u1.sort.i4.why: The fodder crops. They are grown as food for the animals, not for people.
ch12.u1.sort.i5.label: Groundnut
ch12.u1.sort.i5.why: It is a legume and it is grown as an oil seed, which is the group the chapter puts it in.
ask.ch12-u1-sort-2.why.q: Why group crops by what they give us rather than by what they look like?
ask.ch12-u1-sort-2.why.a:
Because the grouping has to be useful for the decision being made, and here the decision is what to plant.

A botanist groups plants by how they are related, and by that test groundnut sits with gram and pea, because all three are legumes. A farmer deciding what to sow is not asking what the plant is related to. They are asking what comes off it, and groundnut comes off as oil.

So the chapter groups it with sesame and mustard, which are not related to it at all. Neither grouping is wrong. They answer different questions, and this one answers the farmer’s.
a.ch12-u1-sort-2.title: What each group of crops is grown for
a.ch12-u1-sort-2.blurb: Six groups, and what we actually take from each.

ch12.u1.quiz.q0.o0: It is already intensively cultivated, with little scope for more area

ch12.u1.quiz.q0.f1: There is no such law. The land is simply already in use.
ch12.u1.quiz.q0.o2: There is plenty of land, but nobody wants to farm it
ch12.u1.quiz.q0.f2: The constraint is land, not willingness.
ch12.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: What does sustainable practice mean in agriculture?
ch12.u1.quiz.q1.o0: Raising production without degrading the land, water and environment it depends on
ch12.u1.quiz.q1.f0: Right. The green revolution raised yields and used natural resources harder, and that is the balance to hold.
ch12.u1.quiz.q1.o1: Producing as much as possible, as fast as possible
ch12.u1.quiz.q1.f1: That is what damages the resources the next harvest depends on.
ch12.u1.quiz.q1.f2: Machinery is not the issue. How hard the natural resources are pushed is.
ch12.u1.quiz.q2.prompt: Does filling warehouses with grain by itself end hunger?
ch12.u1.quiz.q2.o0: No. People also need the income to buy the food
ch12.u1.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Food security needs availability and access, and most of those without access work in agriculture.
ch12.u1.quiz.q2.o1: Yes, as soon as there is enough grain in store
ch12.u1.quiz.q2.f1: Grain in a warehouse is not food on a plate until someone can pay for it.
ch12.u1.quiz.q2.o2: No, because stored grain cannot be eaten
ch12.u1.quiz.q2.f2: Stored grain is perfectly edible. The problem is reaching the people who need it.
a.ch12-u1-quiz-3.title: Why yields have to rise
ch12.u2.variety:
A farmer choosing seed is choosing a variety, and varieties differ in ways that decide the harvest. Breeders select for a short list of characters:

Higher yield, so more comes off each acre. Improved quality, which means something different in each crop: protein in pulses, oil in oilseeds, baking quality in wheat, keeping quality in fruit.

Resistance to biotic stress, meaning diseases, insects and nematodes, and to abiotic stress, meaning drought, salinity, water logging, heat, cold and frost.

A change in maturity duration. A variety that goes from sowing to harvest faster is cheaper, allows more than one crop in a year, and if it ripens uniformly it is easier to harvest with less lost.

Wider adaptability, so one variety works across different climates and the production is steadier.

Desirable agronomic characteristics, which depend on the crop. Tall and heavily branched is what you want in a fodder crop. Dwarf is what you want in a cereal, because a short plant spends less on stem and more on grain.

There are two ways to get these characters into a crop. Hybridisation means crossing genetically dissimilar plants, and it comes in three kinds depending on how far apart the parents are. Genetic modification means introducing a gene that provides the character directly.
a.ch12-u2-read-1.title: Making a variety that does what you need
ch12.u2.sort.i0.label: A fungal disease spreading through a wheat field

ch12.u2.sort.i1.label: Drought through a failed monsoon

ch12.u2.sort.i2.why: Nematodes are small worms, and they are alive.
ch12.u2.sort.i3.label: Salty soil near the coast
ch12.u2.sort.i3.why: A chemical condition of the soil.
ch12.u2.sort.i4.label: A field left water-logged after heavy rain
ch12.u2.sort.i4.why: Too much water is a stress just as too little is.
ch12.u2.sort.i5.label: Insects eating the leaves

ch12.u2.sort.i6.why: Cold, and nothing alive about it.

ask.ch12-u2-tree-3.gm.q: Is a genetically modified crop just a very distant cross?
ask.ch12-u2-tree-3.gm.a:
No, and the difference is worth being clear about.

Hybridisation of any of the three kinds is still two plants crossing, with all the mixing of thousands of genes that implies. The breeder then selects, over several generations, for the plants that happen to have come out well.

Genetic modification puts one known gene for one known character into the crop directly. It does not need the two organisms to be able to cross at all, which is why a gene can come from a bacterium.

The chapter mentions it in a sentence and leaves the argument about it alone, which is a fair reflection of a debate that is still running.
a.ch12-u2-tree-3.title: Which kind of cross?
a.ch12-u2-tree-3.blurb: Hybridisation is named by how far apart the two parents are. One question settles it.
ch12.u2.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and it is intervarietal, interspecific or intergeneric depending on how far apart the parents are.
ch12.u2.quiz.q0.o1: Growing two crops in the same field
ch12.u2.quiz.q0.f1: That is mixed cropping, which is a cropping pattern rather than a breeding method.
ch12.u2.quiz.q0.o2: Adding fertiliser to improve a crop
ch12.u2.quiz.q0.f2: Fertiliser feeds the crop you already have. It does not change the variety.

ch12.u2.quiz.q1.o0: A short plant puts less into stem and more into grain
ch12.u2.quiz.q1.f0: Right. In a fodder crop you want the opposite, because there the stem is the product.
ch12.u2.quiz.q1.f1: Water need is not what dwarfness is selected for.
ch12.u2.quiz.q1.o2: Short plants are easier to see
ch12.u2.quiz.q1.f2: Visibility is not an agronomic character.

ch12.u2.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Nothing living is causing it.
ch12.u2.quiz.q2.f1: Insects are alive, so that is biotic.
ch12.u2.quiz.q2.f2: A virus is a biotic agent in this chapter's sense.

ch12.u3.nutrients:
A plant needs sixteen nutrients, and it gets them from three places.

Air supplies carbon and oxygen. Water supplies hydrogen and oxygen. The soil supplies the other thirteen, and those are the ones a farmer has any say over.

Six of the thirteen are needed in large quantities and are called macro-nutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.

The remaining seven are needed in small quantities and are called micro-nutrients: iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper, molybdenum and chlorine. Small does not mean optional. A crop short of zinc is in trouble just as surely as one short of nitrogen.

A shortage of any of them shows up in growth, in reproduction, and in how easily the plant catches a disease. Supplying them is what manure and fertiliser are for.
a.ch12-u3-read-1.title: Sixteen nutrients, three sources
ch12.u3.sort.i0.label: Carbon
ch12.u3.sort.i0.why: Air supplies it, which is why a plant builds itself largely out of the atmosphere.
ch12.u3.sort.i1.label: Hydrogen
ch12.u3.sort.i2.label: Nitrogen
ch12.u3.sort.i2.why: One of the six needed in quantity, and the one fertilisers are mostly about.
ch12.u3.sort.i3.label: Phosphorus
ch12.u3.sort.i4.label: Potassium
ch12.u3.sort.i5.label: Zinc
ch12.u3.sort.i5.why: Needed in small amounts, and still essential.
ch12.u3.sort.i6.label: Molybdenum
ch12.u3.sort.i7.label: Oxygen
a.ch12-u3-sort-2.title: Where does the plant get it?
ch12.u3.sort2.i0.label: Made by decomposing animal excreta and plant waste
ch12.u3.sort2.i0.why: Cow dung, vegetable refuse, straw and eradicated weeds, left to rot in a pit.
ch12.u3.sort2.i1.label: Produced commercially in a factory
ch12.u3.sort2.i1.why: Which is why it can be supplied at a known concentration.
ch12.u3.sort2.i2.label: Supplies a large quantity of organic matter
ch12.u3.sort2.i2.why: The bulk of it is organic matter, and that is most of what it does for the soil.
ch12.u3.sort2.i3.label: Supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium at high concentration
ch12.u3.sort2.i3.why: A small quantity carries a lot of nutrient, which is why it is easy to overdo.
ch12.u3.sort2.i4.label: Improves the water holding capacity of sandy soil and the drainage of clayey soil
ch12.u3.sort2.i4.why: Because it improves the structure of the soil rather than only its chemistry.
ch12.u3.sort2.i5.label: Can be washed away by excessive irrigation and pollute water
ch12.u3.sort2.i5.why: Which is a loss to the farmer and a problem for everyone downstream.
ch12.u3.sort2.i6.label: Heavy continuous use can destroy soil fertility
ch12.u3.sort2.i6.why: The organic matter is not replaced and the micro-organisms in the soil are harmed.
ch12.u3.sort2.i7.label: Recycles farm waste rather than throwing it away
ch12.u3.sort2.i7.why: Which is an advantage on the farm and in the environment at the same time.
ask.ch12-u3-sort-3.both.q: If manure is so much better, why does anyone use fertiliser?
ask.ch12-u3-sort-3.both.a:
Because they do different jobs, and the high yields of modern farming need the one manure cannot supply.

Manure is bulky and its nutrient content is low and variable. Getting enough nitrogen onto a field from manure alone means moving and spreading an enormous quantity of it, and a farmer who has a few cattle does not have that much.

Fertiliser supplies exactly the nutrient wanted, in a known amount, at the moment the crop needs it. That precision is a real advantage and it is a large part of why yields rose.

The chapter's answer is not to pick one. It is to weigh the short-term benefit of fertiliser against the long-term benefit of manure, and most careful farming uses both.
a.ch12-u3-sort-3.title: Manure or fertiliser?
a.ch12-u3-sort-3.blurb: They both supply nutrients and they do almost nothing else in common.
ch12.u3.irrigation:
Most agriculture in India is rain-fed, which means the harvest depends on the monsoon arriving on time and spreading through the season. A poor monsoon means crop failure, and that is why so much effort goes into irrigation.

The systems in use depend on what water is available nearby.

Wells, of two kinds. A dug well collects water from the water-bearing strata near the surface. A tube well reaches deeper strata. Pumps lift the water from either.

Canals, which are the elaborate option. Water comes from a reservoir or a river into a main canal, which divides into branch canals and then into distributaries that reach the fields.

River lift systems, used where canal flow is unreliable. Water is drawn directly from the river for fields close to it.

Tanks, which are small storage reservoirs catching the run-off from a local catchment.

Two newer ideas matter as much as any of these. Rainwater harvesting and watershed management build small check-dams, which stop rainwater running away, raise the ground water level and reduce soil erosion at the same time.
a.ch12-u3-read-4.title: Water, and where it comes from

ch12.u3.quiz.q0.f1: The size of the molecule has nothing to do with it.
ch12.u3.quiz.q0.o2: Because they are only found in large plants
ch12.u3.quiz.q0.f2: All plants need them, large or small.

ch12.u3.quiz.q1.f0: Right. That is what improves water holding in sandy soil and drainage in clayey soil.

ch12.u3.quiz.q1.o2: A faster effect on the crop
ch12.u3.quiz.q1.f2: Fertiliser acts faster. Manure is the slow one.

ch12.u3.quiz.q2.o0: It stops rainwater running away, raises the ground water and reduces erosion
ch12.u3.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Three benefits from one small structure, which is why watershed management works.
ch12.u3.quiz.q2.o1: It stores water for a single season only
ch12.u3.quiz.q2.f1: Its main effect is on the ground water, which lasts beyond one season.
ch12.u3.quiz.q2.o2: It replaces the need for any other irrigation
ch12.u3.quiz.q2.f2: It supplements other systems rather than replacing them.

ch12.u4.patterns:
Three ways of arranging crops, and they are easy to confuse because all three involve more than one crop.

Mixed cropping is growing two or more crops on the same piece of land at the same time, with no particular arrangement. Wheat with gram, wheat with mustard, groundnut with sunflower. The point is insurance: if one crop fails the other may not, so the whole season is not lost.

Inter-cropping is also two crops at the same time, but in a definite pattern: a few rows of one alternating with a few rows of the other. Soyabean with maize, or bajra with lobia. The two are chosen to need different nutrients, so neither is competing with the other for the same thing, and the rows slow a pest or disease down because it cannot spread through a continuous stand of one crop.

Crop rotation is different in kind: it is about time rather than space. Different crops are grown on the same land one after another, in a planned succession. Done properly it allows two or three crops a year with good harvests. What can follow what is decided by the moisture available and the irrigation.

Mixed farming is different again, and is about the farm rather than the field: crops and livestock on the same holding, so that each supports the other.
a.ch12-u4-read-1.title: What to plant beside what
ch12.u4.sort.i0.label: Wheat and gram sown together across the same field
ch12.u4.sort.i0.why: Both at once, with no particular arrangement. The aim is insurance against one failing.
ch12.u4.sort.i1.label: A few rows of soyabean alternating with a few rows of maize
ch12.u4.sort.i1.why: Both at once, in a definite pattern, chosen so their nutrient needs differ.
ch12.u4.sort.i2.label: A pulse grown after a cereal on the same land the following season
ch12.u4.sort.i2.why: One after the other, in a planned succession.
ch12.u4.sort.i3.label: Two or three crops grown on a piece of land in one year, in a planned order
ch12.u4.sort.i3.why: The planned succession is what makes it rotation rather than anything else.
ch12.u4.sort.i4.label: Bajra and lobia in alternating strips
ch12.u4.sort.i4.why: A definite row pattern, so this is inter-cropping rather than mixed cropping.
ch12.u4.sort.i5.label: Groundnut and sunflower scattered together on one plot
ch12.u4.sort.i5.why: At the same time and with no row pattern.
ask.ch12-u4-sort-2.whyrows.q: If both crops are grown at once, why do the rows matter?
ask.ch12-u4-sort-2.whyrows.a:
Because rows let you choose which plants are neighbours, and that is where the benefit comes from.

Inter-cropping pairs crops whose nutrient needs differ, so a row of one is not taking the same thing out of the soil as the row beside it. Scatter them and the same pairing happens by accident in some places and not in others.

Rows also slow down a pest or a disease. An insect that has found its crop has to cross a strip of something it does not eat to find more, and many do not manage it. In a scattered mixture there is no strip to cross.

Mixed cropping gives up both of those and keeps the one that matters most to a farmer with little margin: if one crop fails, the season is not lost.
a.ch12-u4-sort-2.title: Which pattern is it?
a.ch12-u4-sort-2.blurb: Two at once with no pattern, two at once in rows, or one after another.
ch12.u4.protection:
A field crop is attacked from three directions, and then attacked again after it is cut.

Weeds are unwanted plants growing with the crop, such as Xanthium, Parthenium and Cyperinus rotundus. They take nutrients, space and light, and the crucial time to remove them is early, while the crop is young.

Insect pests attack in three distinct ways, and this list is worth holding: they cut the root, stem and leaf; they suck the cell sap from various parts; and they bore into stem and fruits.

Diseases are caused by pathogens, meaning bacteria, fungi and viruses, which come through the soil, the water and the air.

All three can be controlled with pesticides: herbicides for weeds, insecticides for insects and fungicides for fungi. Used in excess they become a problem of their own, because they are poisonous to many species and pollute the environment.

So preventive methods come first. Proper seed bed preparation, timely sowing, inter-cropping, crop rotation, resistant varieties and summer ploughing, which turns the soil deep in the hot months and destroys pests and weeds in it.

After the harvest the losses continue. In storage, the biotic agents are insects, rodents, fungi, mites and bacteria, and the abiotic ones are inappropriate moisture and temperature. They cost weight, germinability, colour and therefore price. The answers are strict cleaning before storage, drying the produce first in sunlight and then in shade, fumigation, and systematic management of the warehouse.

ch12.u5.cattle:
Animal husbandry is the scientific management of livestock: feeding, breeding and disease control. Cattle husbandry is done for two purposes, and the words matter.

Milch animals are the milk-producing females, which is what dairy means. Draught animals are the ones used for labour: tilling, irrigation and carting. Indian cattle belong to two species, Bos indicus for cows and Bos bubalis for buffaloes.

Milk production depends largely on the lactation period, which is how long an animal gives milk after a calf is born. A longer lactation means more milk from the same animal.

Exotic breeds such as Jersey and Brown Swiss have long lactation periods. Local breeds such as Red Sindhi and Sahiwal have excellent resistance to disease. Cross-breeding the two is how an animal with both is obtained, and that is the usual answer when an exercise asks how cattle breeds are improved.

Good management is specific. Clean, well-ventilated roofed sheds that keep off rain, heat and cold. A sloping floor so it stays dry and can be cleaned. Regular brushing to remove dirt and loose hair.

Feed is of two kinds and the animal needs both: roughage, which is largely fibre, and concentrates, which are low in fibre and high in protein and other nutrients. Both are needed in proportionate amounts, and feed additives with micronutrients improve health and milk output.

Disease reduces milk as well as causing suffering. External parasites live on the skin and cause skin disease; internal parasites such as worms affect the stomach and intestine, and flukes damage the liver. Bacteria and viruses cause infectious diseases, and vaccination exists for many of them.
a.ch12-u5-read-1.title: Cattle, and what management means
ch12.u5.sort.bin.2: Neither: this is management, not breeding
ch12.u5.sort.i0.label: A long lactation period
ch12.u5.sort.i0.why: Jersey and Brown Swiss give milk for longer after a calf is born.
ch12.u5.sort.i1.label: Excellent resistance to disease
ch12.u5.sort.i1.why: Red Sindhi and Sahiwal, bred over centuries in this climate.
ch12.u5.sort.i2.label: A sloping shed floor that stays dry
ch12.u5.sort.i2.why: Nothing to do with the animal's ancestry. It is how the shed is built.

ch12.u5.sort.i3.why: The same centuries of selection that gave it the disease resistance.
ch12.u5.sort.i4.label: Regular brushing to remove dirt and loose hair
ch12.u5.sort.i4.why: A daily practice, not an inherited character.

ask.ch12-u5-sort-2.justexotic.q: If exotic breeds give more milk, why not simply keep exotic cattle?
ask.ch12-u5-sort-2.justexotic.a:
Because the yield is only one of the numbers, and the others go the wrong way.

A Jersey in an Indian summer is a Jersey in the wrong climate. It suffers in the heat, it catches diseases that a Sahiwal shrugs off, and it needs better feed, better shelter and more veterinary attention to give the yield it is capable of. A smallholder who cannot supply all of that gets a sick animal rather than a productive one.

A cross keeps most of the lactation period and most of the resistance. It is not as good as either parent at the thing that parent is best at, and it is the animal that actually survives and produces on an ordinary farm.
a.ch12-u5-sort-2.title: Why cross an exotic breed with a local one?
a.ch12-u5-sort-2.blurb: Each parent is brought in for something the other does not have.
ch12.u5.poultry:
Poultry farming raises domestic fowl for two different products, and the two need different birds and different management.

Layers are kept for eggs. Broilers are raised for meat.

Improvement comes from cross-breeding Indian breeds, such as Aseel, with exotic ones, such as Leghorn. The traits bred for are: the number and quality of chicks; a dwarf broiler parent for commercial chick production; summer adaptation and tolerance of high temperature; low maintenance requirements; and a smaller egg-laying bird able to live on cheaper, more fibrous diets made from agricultural by-products.

That last one is the striking fact of the whole section. Poultry turns low-fibre material unfit for people into highly nutritious animal protein.

Broilers and layers are fed differently. A broiler's daily ration is rich in protein with adequate fat, and the vitamin A and vitamin K levels in the feed are kept high. Broilers are also given vitamin-rich supplementary feed for growth and feed efficiency, and care is taken over feathering and carcass quality. Their housing, nutrition and environment differ from those of egg layers.

Both suffer from diseases caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites, and from nutritional deficiencies. The answers are proper cleaning, sanitation, spraying of disinfectants at regular intervals, and appropriate vaccination.
a.ch12-u5-read-3.title: Layers and broilers
ch12.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: What is the difference between a milch animal and a draught animal?
ch12.u5.quiz.q0.o0: Milch animals produce milk and draught animals are used for labour
ch12.u5.quiz.q0.f0: Right. It is what the animal is kept for, not what it is.
ch12.u5.quiz.q0.o1: Milch animals are cows and draught animals are buffaloes
ch12.u5.quiz.q0.f1: Both species supply both kinds. The division is by purpose.
ch12.u5.quiz.q0.o2: Milch animals are exotic and draught animals are local
ch12.u5.quiz.q0.f2: Ancestry does not decide the purpose.
ch12.u5.quiz.q1.prompt: Why are exotic and local cattle breeds cross-bred?
ch12.u5.quiz.q1.o0: To get long lactation from one and disease resistance from the other
ch12.u5.quiz.q1.f0: Right, and this is the standard answer when an exercise asks how breeds are improved.
ch12.u5.quiz.q1.f1: Size is not what either parent is being brought in for.
ch12.u5.quiz.q1.o2: Because local breeds give no milk
ch12.u5.quiz.q1.f2: Local breeds give milk. They give it for a shorter period.
ch12.u5.quiz.q2.prompt: What is the difference between layers and broilers?
ch12.u5.quiz.q2.o0: Layers are kept for eggs and broilers are raised for meat
ch12.u5.quiz.q2.f0: Right, and their housing, feed and management all differ accordingly.
ch12.u5.quiz.q2.o1: Layers are female and broilers are male
ch12.u5.quiz.q2.f1: Sex is not the distinction being drawn here.
ch12.u5.quiz.q2.o2: Layers are indigenous and broilers are exotic
ch12.u5.quiz.q2.f2: Both come from cross-breeding programmes between Indian and exotic breeds.
a.ch12-u5-quiz-4.title: Cattle and poultry
ch12.u6.fish:
Fish is a cheap source of animal protein, and the word covers both true finned fish and shellfish such as prawns and molluscs.

There are two ways of getting it, and the distinction runs through the whole topic. Capture fishing takes fish from natural stocks. Culture fishery grows them, which is fish farming. Either can be done in seawater or in fresh water, so there are four combinations and the chapter gives each a name.

Marine fisheries. India has 7500 km of coastline and the deep seas beyond it. Popular marine varieties include pomphret, mackerel, tuna, sardines and Bombay duck. They are caught with fishing nets from boats, and yields are raised by locating large schools with satellites and echo-sounders. Some high-value species are farmed in seawater instead: mullets, bhetki, pearl spots, prawns, mussels and oysters, and oysters are also grown for pearls. Farming in the sea is called mariculture, and as wild stocks are depleted it is the only way the demand can be met.

Inland fisheries. Fresh water means canals, ponds, reservoirs and rivers; brackish water, where seawater and fresh water mix, means estuaries and lagoons. Capture fishing happens here too and the yield is not high, so most inland production comes from aquaculture.

The clever part is composite fish culture. Five or six species are kept in one pond, chosen so that they do not compete: Catlas feed at the surface, Rohus in the middle, Mrigals and Common Carps at the bottom, and Grass Carps on the weeds. Together they use all the food in the pond, and the yield goes up.

Its one real problem is seed. Many of these fish breed only during the monsoon, and seed collected from the wild is mixed with other species. Hormonal stimulation is now used to breed them in ponds, which gives pure seed in the quantity wanted.
a.ch12-u6-read-1.title: Caught, or farmed
ch12.u6.sort.i0.label: Catla
ch12.u6.sort.i0.why: Which leaves the rest of the pond to everyone else.
ch12.u6.sort.i1.label: Rohu
ch12.u6.sort.i1.why: Between the surface feeder and the bottom feeders.
ch12.u6.sort.i2.label: Mrigal
ch12.u6.sort.i3.label: Common carp
ch12.u6.sort.i3.why: Sharing the bottom with the mrigal.
ch12.u6.sort.i4.label: Grass carp
ch12.u6.sort.i4.why: Which also keeps the pond clear, so it does two jobs.
ch12.u6.sort.i5.label: Silver carp
ch12.u6.sort.i5.why: Another surface feeder, which is why stocking is planned rather than guessed.
ask.ch12-u6-sort-2.seed.q: If composite culture works so well, what is holding it back?
ask.ch12-u6-sort-2.seed.a:
Seed, and only seed.

Most of these species breed only during the monsoon, so there is one short window a year when fry can be collected from rivers and ponds. What is collected is a mixture: you set out for catla and come back with catla, some rohu and a good deal of whatever else was spawning.

A pond stocked with the wrong proportions loses the whole advantage, because two surface feeders compete for the same food while the bottom goes unused.

The fix is hormonal stimulation, which makes the fish breed in a pond when the farmer wants them to. That gives pure seed of each species in the quantity needed, and it is what turned composite culture from a good idea into a practice.
a.ch12-u6-sort-2.title: Who eats where in the pond?
a.ch12-u6-sort-2.blurb: This is the whole idea of composite fish culture: five mouths, five different places.
ch12.u6.bees:
Bee-keeping is kept for last because it is the clearest case of the chapter's argument. It needs very little investment, it fits alongside whatever else a farmer is doing, and it produces two saleable things: honey, and the wax from the hives, which is used in medicinal preparations.

The local varieties used for commercial honey production are Apis cerana indica, commonly called the Indian bee, along with A. dorsata, the rock bee, and A. florae. An Italian variety, A. mellifera, has been brought in to raise the yield.

The Italian bee is the one usually kept commercially, for a specific set of reasons: it collects a lot of honey, it stings somewhat less, it stays in a given hive for long periods rather than absconding, and it breeds very well.

Hives are kept together in an apiary, which is a bee farm.

The value and the quality of the honey depend on the pasturage: the flowers available to the bees for nectar and pollen. Quantity of pasturage decides how much honey there is, and the kind of flowers decides what it tastes like. A farmer who knows what is flowering nearby knows what the honey will be.
a.ch12-u6-read-3.title: Bees
ch12.u6.quiz.q0.prompt: What is the difference between capture fishing and culture fishery?
ch12.u6.quiz.q0.o0: Capture fishing takes fish from natural stocks and culture fishery grows them
ch12.u6.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and either can be done in seawater or in fresh water.
ch12.u6.quiz.q0.o1: Capture fishing is in the sea and culture fishery is in fresh water
ch12.u6.quiz.q0.f1: Both happen in both. Mariculture is farming in the sea.
ch12.u6.quiz.q0.o2: Capture fishing uses nets and culture fishery uses lines
ch12.u6.quiz.q0.f2: The equipment is not the distinction.
ch12.u6.quiz.q1.prompt: Why are five or six species kept together in composite fish culture?
ch12.u6.quiz.q1.o0: They feed in different parts of the pond, so all the food is used without competition
ch12.u6.quiz.q1.f0: Right: surface, middle, bottom and weeds, all used at once.
ch12.u6.quiz.q1.o1: They breed with each other and give a better fish
ch12.u6.quiz.q1.f1: They are not cross-bred. They are chosen not to compete.
ch12.u6.quiz.q1.o2: A larger number of species looks better to a buyer
ch12.u6.quiz.q1.f2: The reason is the food in the pond, not the market.
ch12.u6.quiz.q2.o0: The flowers available to the bees for nectar and pollen
ch12.u6.quiz.q2.f0: Right, and both the quantity of honey and its taste depend on it.
ch12.u6.quiz.q2.o1: The field where the hives are placed
ch12.u6.quiz.q2.f1: That is the apiary. Pasturage is what is flowering within reach of it.
ch12.u6.quiz.q2.o2: The feed given to the bees by the keeper
ch12.u6.quiz.q2.f2: Bees collect their own. Pasturage is what there is to collect.
a.ch12-u6-quiz-4.title: Fish and bees
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.goal: A one-hectare field is giving 20 quintals of wheat. Get it to 32 or more, and be ready to say where each gain comes from. The question at the end of section 12.1.3 asks exactly this.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.variety.label: Sow a high-yielding variety bred for this district
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.variety.because: A variety selected for yield and for the local climate produces more per acre, and that gain costs nothing extra every season.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.variety.wrong: A high-yielding variety grows larger plants, so there is more of everything including the stem.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.fertiliser.labe: Apply fertiliser at the recommended dose, at the right time
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.fertiliser.beca: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium at a known dose, timed to when the crop needs them, so that the plant takes them up instead of the rain carrying them off.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.fertiliser.wron: Fertiliser is plant food, so more of it in the soil always means more grain.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.manure.label: Work ten tonnes of farmyard manure into the hectare
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.manure.because: Organic matter improves the structure of the soil, so it holds water better and drains better, and the nutrients that come with it are a bonus.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.manure.wrong: Manure is a concentrated source of nitrogen, so it does the same job as fertiliser more cheaply.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.irrigation.labe: Irrigate at the crop's critical growth stages rather than by habit
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.irrigation.beca: Water matters most at particular stages of growth. The same water given at the right moment is worth far more than the same water given whenever it is convenient.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.irrigation.wron: A crop needs as much water as it can get, so the more often the field is flooded the better.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.weeding.label: Weed in the first few weeks, before the crop closes over
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.weeding.because: Weeds take nutrients, space and light, and the damage is done while the crop is young and small. Removing them later saves much less.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.weeding.wrong: Weeds are a problem at harvest, because they get mixed into the grain, so weeding is best left until late.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.overdose.label: Apply three times the recommended fertiliser dose
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.overdose.becaus: The crop cannot take up that much. The excess washes away with the irrigation, pollutes the water, and over years the soil loses its organic matter and its micro-organisms.
chal.ch12-u1-challenge-4.overdose.wrong: Three times the dose gives three times the growth, and the only cost is the price of the extra fertiliser.
ch12.u1.challenge.debrief:
Notice that no single change got you there. The question the chapter asks is which combination gives the most benefit, and the answer it wants is all of them together: good seed, irrigation, fertiliser and crop protection.

Notice too that the largest single number on the list is the variety, and that it costs nothing after the seed is bought. That is why crop variety improvement is the first of the three groups of activities and not the last.

And the overdose is on the list for a reason. It is the one option that takes the yield down, and in a real field it keeps taking it down for years after.
a.ch12-u1-challenge-4.title: Get the yield up, and keep it up
a.ch12-u1-challenge-4.blurb: A field giving 20 quintals a hectare. Get it to 32, and be able to say why each thing you change works.
ch12.u4.do.steps:
1. Find a field or garden you are allowed to walk to the edge of. Ask first.
2. Write down what crop is growing, and what season it was sown in.
3. List every plant growing there that is not the crop. Those are the weeds. Photograph or sketch any you cannot name.
4. Look closely at ten plants of the crop. Note any leaves that are cut, any stems with holes, and any leaves that are curled or discoloured.
5. For each kind of damage, decide which of the three ways an insect attacks it matches: cutting, sucking sap, or boring.
6. Ask the farmer two questions: what they do about the weeds, and what they do about the pests.
7. Bring the list back to class and compare it with what everyone else found.
ch12.u4.do.watch: A group that lists only the damage they can name. Unidentified damage is worth more here than a confident wrong label, so insist on a sketch and a question mark rather than a guess.
a.ch12-u4-do-6.title: Go and look at a field
a.ch12-u4-do-6.blurb: A notebook, a field, and an hour. Most of this chapter is visible from the edge of one.
ch12.u4.visit.steps:
1. Choose one: a fish farm, a poultry farm or a bee-keeper. Arrange the visit in advance.
2. Before you go, write your questions down. For a fish farm: which varieties, what kind of ponds, what feed, and how much is produced. For poultry: which breeds, what ration, what housing and lighting, and which birds are layers and which are broilers. For bees: which variety, how many hives, and what is flowering nearby.
3. At the farm, ask your questions and write the answers as they are given, not as you expected them.
4. Ask one more: what is the hardest part of the work, and what would improve it most.
5. If no farm is near you, collect the same information from books, from the internet, or by talking to anyone in your area who keeps animals or fish.
6. Compare the answers in class against what the chapter says. Note anything that does not match, and say why you think it differs.
ch12.u4.visit.watch: The last step is the one that matters. A farmer who does something the book does not mention usually has a reason, and finding out what it is teaches more than the visit itself.
a.ch12-u6-do-4.title: Visit a farm and ask the right questions
a.ch12-u6-do-4.blurb: A fish farm, a poultry shed or an apiary. The questions are the same shape in all three.
mis.law-stops-new-farmland.statement: India cannot farm more land because it is not allowed to.
mis.law-stops-new-farmland.correction: There is no such law. The land is already intensively cultivated and there is very little left to bring in.
mis.land-is-available.statement: There is plenty of uncultivated land left in India.
mis.land-is-available.correction: There is no major scope for increasing the area under cultivation, which is why the chapter is about efficiency.
mis.sustainable-means-maximum.statement: Sustainable farming means producing as much as possible.
mis.sustainable-means-maximum.correction: It means raising production without degrading the soil, water and environment the next harvest depends on.
mis.sustainable-means-no-machines.statem: Sustainable farming means farming without machinery.
mis.sustainable-means-no-machines.correc: Machinery is not the issue. How hard the natural resources are pushed is.
mis.storage-ends-hunger.statement: Filling warehouses with grain ends hunger.
mis.storage-ends-hunger.correction: People also need the income to buy it, and most of those without that income work in agriculture.
mis.stored-grain-is-useless.statement: Grain in a warehouse is of no use.
mis.stored-grain-is-useless.correction: It is perfectly good food. The difficulty is getting it to the people who cannot pay for it.
mis.hybridisation-is-mixed-cropping.stat: Hybridisation means growing two crops in the same field.
mis.hybridisation-is-mixed-cropping.corr: That is mixed cropping. Hybridisation is crossing two genetically dissimilar plants to make a new variety.
mis.hybridisation-is-fertilising.stateme: Hybridisation means improving a crop by feeding it better.
mis.hybridisation-is-fertilising.correct: Fertiliser feeds the crop you already have. Hybridisation changes what crop you have.
mis.dwarf-saves-water.statement: Dwarf cereals are bred because short plants need less water.
mis.dwarf-saves-water.correction: They are bred because a short plant puts less into stem and more into grain.
mis.dwarf-is-for-visibility.statement: Dwarf cereals are bred so that the field is easier to see across.
mis.dwarf-is-for-visibility.correction: They are bred because a short plant spends less on stem and more on grain. Nobody selects a crop for the view.
mis.insects-are-abiotic.statement: Insect attack is an abiotic stress.
mis.insects-are-abiotic.correction: Insects are alive, so it is biotic. Abiotic means drought, salinity, water logging, heat, cold and frost.
mis.disease-is-abiotic.statement: Plant disease is an abiotic stress.
mis.disease-is-abiotic.correction: Bacteria, fungi and viruses are biotic agents, and so the stress they cause is biotic.
mis.macro-means-large-molecule.statement: Macro-nutrients are called that because their molecules are large.
mis.macro-means-large-molecule.correctio: They are called that because plants need them in large quantities. Molecule size has nothing to do with it.
mis.macro-means-large-plants.statement: Macro-nutrients are the ones needed by large plants.
mis.macro-means-large-plants.correction: Every plant needs all sixteen. The division is by quantity needed, not by the size of the plant.
mis.micro-means-optional.statement: Micro-nutrients are optional, because so little is needed.
mis.micro-means-optional.correction: A crop short of zinc is in trouble just as surely as one short of nitrogen. Small quantity, not small importance.
mis.only-manure-has-nitrogen.correction: Both supply it. Fertiliser supplies far more of it per kilogram, which is most of the point of fertiliser.
mis.manure-acts-faster.statement: Manure acts faster on a crop than fertiliser does.
mis.manure-acts-faster.correction: Fertiliser is the quick one. Manure works slowly, and does its real work on the soil rather than on one crop.
mis.fertiliser-is-always-better.statemen: Fertiliser is simply a better version of manure.
mis.fertiliser-is-always-better.correcti: They do different jobs. Fertiliser supplies a precise nutrient dose; manure supplies organic matter and soil structure, which fertiliser cannot.
mis.check-dam-is-seasonal.statement: A check-dam only stores water for one season.
mis.check-dam-is-seasonal.correction: Its main effect is on the ground water level, which lasts well beyond one season, and it reduces soil erosion at the same time.
mis.check-dam-replaces-irrigation.statem: A check-dam removes the need for any other irrigation.
mis.check-dam-replaces-irrigation.correc: It supplements wells, canals and tanks rather than replacing them.
mis.mixed-cropping-is-rotation.statement: Mixed cropping means growing crops one after another.
mis.mixed-cropping-is-rotation.correctio: That is crop rotation. Mixed cropping grows two or more crops at the same time on the same land.
mis.intercropping-is-one-crop.statement: Inter-cropping means growing a single crop in rows.
mis.intercropping-is-one-crop.correction: Inter means between, and it takes two crops to have a between: a few rows of one alternating with a few rows of another.
mis.groundnut-is-a-pulse.statement: Groundnut is grouped with the pulses, because it is a legume.
mis.groundnut-is-a-pulse.correction: The chapter groups it with the oil seeds, because that is what it is grown for.
mis.pests-eat-seed-flower-root.statement: Insect pests attack by eating the seed, the flower and the root.
mis.pests-eat-seed-flower-root.correctio: The chapter's three are cutting root, stem and leaf; sucking cell sap; and boring into stem and fruits.
mis.pests-spread-pathogens.statement: Insect pests damage crops by spreading bacteria, fungi and viruses.
mis.pests-spread-pathogens.correction: Those are pathogens and they cause disease, which is a separate attack. Insects do their own damage directly.
mis.pesticides-fail-on-weeds.statement: Pesticides do not work on weeds.
mis.pesticides-fail-on-weeds.correction: Herbicides are pesticides and they work on weeds. The objection to excessive use is poisoning and pollution, not failure.
mis.prevention-is-quicker.statement: Preventive methods are preferred because they are quicker than pesticides.
mis.prevention-is-quicker.correction: They are slower and need planning. They are preferred because heavy pesticide use poisons other species and pollutes.
mis.milch-means-cow.statement: Milch animals are cows and draught animals are buffaloes.
mis.milch-means-cow.correction: Both species supply both. The division is by what the animal is kept for: milk, or labour.
mis.milch-means-exotic.statement: Milch animals are exotic breeds and draught animals are local ones.
mis.milch-means-exotic.correction: Ancestry does not decide purpose. A local cow can be a milch animal and often is.
mis.crossbreeding-is-for-size.statement: Exotic and local cattle are cross-bred to make larger animals.
mis.crossbreeding-is-for-size.correction: They are cross-bred to combine the exotic breed's long lactation with the local breed's disease resistance.
mis.local-breeds-give-no-milk.statement: Local cattle breeds give no milk.
mis.local-breeds-give-no-milk.correction: They give milk, for a shorter lactation period, and they resist disease far better.
mis.layers-and-broilers-by-sex.statement: Layers are female birds and broilers are male.
mis.layers-and-broilers-by-sex.correctio: Layers are kept for eggs and broilers are raised for meat. That is the distinction.
mis.layers-and-broilers-by-origin.statem: Layers are indigenous breeds and broilers are exotic.
mis.layers-and-broilers-by-origin.correc: Both come from cross-breeding programmes between Indian and exotic breeds.
mis.capture-means-marine.statement: Capture fishing means fishing in the sea and culture fishery means fresh water.
mis.capture-means-marine.correction: Either can be done in either. Capture takes from natural stocks and culture grows the fish, and farming in the sea is mariculture.
mis.capture-is-about-equipment.statement: The difference between capture fishing and culture fishery is the equipment used.
mis.capture-is-about-equipment.correctio: It is whether the fish were grown or taken from a natural stock.
mis.composite-is-for-breeding.statement: Several species are kept together in a pond so that they breed with each other.
mis.composite-is-for-breeding.correction: They are chosen so that they do not compete, feeding at different levels of the pond. They are not cross-bred.
mis.composite-is-for-market.statement: Several species are kept together because buyers prefer a variety.
mis.composite-is-for-market.correction: The reason is the food in the pond. Five species feeding at five levels use all of it.
mis.pasturage-is-the-apiary.statement: Pasturage is the field where the hives are kept.
mis.pasturage-is-the-apiary.correction: That is the apiary. Pasturage is the flowers available to the bees for nectar and pollen.
mis.pasturage-is-supplied-feed.statement: Pasturage is the feed a bee-keeper gives the bees.
mis.pasturage-is-supplied-feed.correctio: Bees collect their own. Pasturage is what there is within reach for them to collect.
tree.cross.root.label: A cross between two plants
tree.cross.root.q: How far apart are the two parents?
tree.cross.root.o0: Two varieties of the same crop
tree.cross.root.o1: Two species of the same genus
tree.cross.intervarietal.label: Intervarietal
tree.cross.interspecific.label: Interspecific
tree.cross.intergeneric.label: Intergeneric
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: Explain why India has to raise yields rather than simply farm more land.
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: The land is already intensively cultivated, so there is no major scope for increasing the area. More than a billion people need a quarter of a billion tonnes of grain a year, and it has to come off the land already in use.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'there is plenty of spare land'. There is not, and that single fact is why the rest of the chapter exists.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: Name the three groups of activities that improve crop yields.
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: Crop variety improvement, crop production management and crop protection management. Choosing the seed, nurturing the plant, and protecting the crop growing and harvested.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for only the first two. Protection after the harvest is routinely forgotten, and storage losses are large.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: What is hybridisation, and what are its three kinds?
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: Crossing genetically dissimilar plants. Intervarietal, between different varieties; interspecific, between two species of the same genus; and intergeneric, between different genera.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for hybridisation being confused with mixed cropping. One makes a new variety and the other arranges two existing crops in a field.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: Give two examples of biotic stress and two of abiotic stress on a crop.
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: Biotic: diseases, insects, nematodes. Abiotic: drought, salinity, water logging, heat, cold, frost. Biotic means caused by something living.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for water logging being called biotic because it harms the plant. The test is whether the cause is alive, not whether the effect is bad.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Name the macro-nutrients a plant takes from the soil, and say why they are called that.
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur. They are called macro because the plant needs them in large quantities, not because they matter more than the micro-nutrients.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for micro-nutrients being described as optional. A crop short of zinc is in trouble just as surely as one short of nitrogen.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: Compare manure and fertiliser as ways of keeping soil fertile.
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: Manure is decomposed plant and animal waste. It supplies small quantities of nutrients and a great deal of organic matter, which improves soil structure, water holding in sandy soil and drainage in clayey soil. Fertiliser is made commercially and supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium at high concentration, with no organic matter. It acts faster, it washes away and pollutes water, and continuous heavy use can destroy fertility.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for fertiliser described as simply a better manure. They do different jobs, and the choice is between a short-term benefit and a long-term one.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Describe the difference between mixed cropping, inter-cropping and crop rotation.
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: Mixed cropping is two or more crops at the same time on the same land, with no pattern, as insurance against one failing. Inter-cropping is two crops at the same time in a definite row pattern, chosen for different nutrient needs. Crop rotation is different crops one after another in a planned succession.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for mixed cropping and crop rotation being swapped. One is about space and the other about time, and that is the quickest way to hold them apart.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: Name the three ways insect pests attack a crop.
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: They cut the root, stem and leaf; they suck the cell sap from various parts; and they bore into the stem and the fruits.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for pathogens being offered instead. Bacteria, fungi and viruses cause disease, which the chapter treats as a separate attack.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: Explain why exotic and local cattle breeds are cross-bred.
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: Exotic breeds such as Jersey and Brown Swiss have long lactation periods. Local breeds such as Red Sindhi and Sahiwal resist disease well. Crossing them gives an animal with both.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'to make bigger animals'. Size is not what either parent is brought in for, and the exercise asks for the two specific qualities.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: What is the difference between layers and broilers, and in how they are managed?
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: Layers are kept for eggs and broilers are raised for meat. Broilers get a protein-rich ration with adequate fat and high vitamin A and K, plus vitamin-rich supplementary feed, and their housing and environment differ from those of layers.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for the two being distinguished by sex or by breed. It is what the bird is kept for.
recap.s.u6.q1.ask: Describe how capture fishing, mariculture and aquaculture differ.
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: Capture fishing takes fish from natural stocks. Mariculture is farming them in seawater. Aquaculture is farming them in fresh or brackish water. The first is about taking; the other two are about growing.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Listen for capture being equated with the sea. Capture fishing happens in rivers and ponds too, and farming happens in the sea.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: Explain why five or six fish species are kept together in composite fish culture.
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: Because they feed in different parts of the pond and so do not compete. Catlas at the surface, Rohus in the middle, Mrigals and Common Carps at the bottom, and Grass Carps on the weeds. All the food in the pond gets used and the yield rises.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'so they breed with each other'. They are chosen not to compete, and the real difficulty with the method is getting pure seed of each species.
aid.s.u3.meaning: Five tests that separate manure from fertiliser, and the word is the first thing manure does: it loosens the soil, which is what improves water holding in sand and drainage in clay. Fertiliser changes the chemistry and leaves the structure exactly as it found it.
aid.s.u3.0.property: Life in the soil, over the years
aid.s.u3.0.a: Keeps it. The organic matter feeds the micro-organisms and replaces what the crop took out.
aid.s.u3.0.b: Continuous heavy use harms the micro-organisms and can destroy fertility.
aid.s.u3.1.property: Origin: where did it come from?
aid.s.u3.1.a: Decomposed animal excreta and plant waste, rotted in a pit on the farm.
aid.s.u3.2.property: Organic matter: how much does it add?
aid.s.u3.2.a: A great deal. The bulk of it is organic matter, and that is most of what it does.
aid.s.u3.2.b: None at all. It supplies nutrients and nothing else.
aid.s.u3.3.property: Strength: how concentrated are the nutrients?
aid.s.u3.3.a: Low, and variable. A lot of it has to be spread to supply much.
aid.s.u3.3.b: High and known, which is both its advantage and the reason it is easy to overdo.
aid.s.u3.4.property: Escape: can it be washed away?
aid.s.u3.4.a: Much less. It is bound up in the organic matter.
aid.s.u3.4.b: Readily, by excessive irrigation, and it pollutes the water it ends up in.
gloss.hybridisation: Crossing genetically dissimilar plants to combine their characters. Intervarietal, interspecific or intergeneric, depending on how far apart the parents are.
gloss.variety: A type of a crop selected for particular characters: yield, quality, resistance, maturity duration or adaptability.
gloss.genetic-modification: A crop improved by introducing a gene that provides a desired character directly, rather than by crossing two plants.
gloss.biotic-stress: Damage to a crop caused by living agents: diseases, insects and nematodes.
gloss.abiotic-stress: Damage to a crop caused by non-living conditions: drought, salinity, water logging, heat, cold and frost.
gloss.macro-nutrient: A nutrient a plant needs in large quantity. Six come from the soil: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.
gloss.micro-nutrient: A nutrient a plant needs in small quantity and cannot do without: iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper, molybdenum and chlorine.
gloss.manure: Organic matter from decomposed animal excreta and plant waste. Supplies small quantities of nutrients and a great deal of structure to the soil.
gloss.fertiliser: A commercially produced plant nutrient, supplying nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium at high concentration. Fast acting, and damaging to soil fertility if used heavily for years.
gloss.organic-farming: A system with minimal or no chemical fertilisers, herbicides and pesticides, using organic manure, recycled farm waste and bio-agents instead.
gloss.irrigation: Supplying water to crops. Wells, canals, river lift systems and tanks, with rainwater harvesting and check-dams raising the ground water.
gloss.mixed-cropping: Growing two or more crops on the same land at the same time, with no particular arrangement. Insurance against one of them failing.
gloss.inter-cropping: Growing two or more crops at the same time in a definite row pattern, chosen so that their nutrient needs differ.
gloss.crop-rotation: Growing different crops on the same land one after another, in a planned succession.
gloss.mixed-farming: A farm that raises crops and livestock together, so that each supports the other.
gloss.animal-husbandry: The scientific management of livestock: feeding, breeding and disease control. Covers cattle, goats, sheep, poultry and fish.
gloss.milch-animal: Milch animals are the milk-producing females. Draught animals are the ones used for labour: tilling, irrigation and carting.
gloss.lactation-period: The time an animal produces milk after a calf is born. A longer one means more milk, which is why exotic breeds are brought into a cross.
gloss.poultry-farming: Raising domestic fowl. Layers are kept for eggs and broilers for meat, and the two are housed and fed differently.
gloss.capture-fishing: Taking fish from natural stocks, in the sea or in fresh water, as opposed to growing them.
gloss.mariculture: Culturing fish and shellfish in seawater: mullets, bhetki, pearl spots, prawns, mussels and oysters.
gloss.aquaculture: Growing fish in fresh or brackish water, which is where most inland fish production comes from.
gloss.composite-fish-culture: Keeping five or six species in one pond, chosen to feed at different levels so that none competes and all the food is used.
gloss.apiary: A bee farm: a place where hives are kept together for commercial honey production.
gloss.pasturage: The flowers available to bees for nectar and pollen. Its quantity decides how much honey there is and the kind of flower decides the taste.
